title: A house and its owner
translation: I know a house is only somewhere we stay for a while, but a home that really suits the person living in it is a pleasure. Where someone with taste lives quietly, even the moonlight coming in looks lovelier.

Nothing's fashionable or showy, but the trees are old, the grass in the garden grows the way it wants and still looks thoughtful somehow, the veranda and the bamboo fence are just right, and the furniture is old and comfortable. You see a place like that and want to meet whoever lives there.

Then there's the other kind. A crowd of craftsmen has polished everything to perfection, rare and expensive pieces from China and Japan are on display, and even the garden plants have been forced into shape. It's painful to look at. Sad, really. Is anyone going to live there forever? It could all go up in smoke in a moment. That's the first thing you think.
Mostly, you can tell what someone is like from their house.

Sanesada once had ropes stretched over the roof of his main hall to stop kites from perching on it. When Saigyō saw that, he said, "What harm would a kite do up there? So that's the kind of man he is," and never visited again. I'd heard this story, so when I saw ropes strung along the roof of the Kosaka residence, where the prince of Ayanokōji lives, I thought of it. But someone told me: "Actually, crows were gathering there and catching the frogs in the pond, and the prince saw it and felt sorry for them." I thought that was wonderful.
Maybe Sanesada had his reasons too.

literal: That a dwelling be fitting and as one would wish: though I think it is a temporary lodging, it is a pleasing thing.
In a place where a person of quality lives at ease, even the colour of the moonlight coming in looks especially moving.

Not modern or glittering, but the grove of trees aged, the garden grass that is not contrived looking thoughtful, the arrangement of veranda and openwork fence charming, and the furniture at hand reminiscent of the past and at ease: that looks admirable.

What many craftsmen have polished with all their care, with rare and exquisite furnishings of China and Japan set out, and even the plants of the garden made not as they would naturally grow: it is painful to the eye and very dreary.
Can one go on living like that for long? It will probably become smoke in a moment: so one thinks at the first glance.
Generally, it is from the dwelling that a person's character can be guessed.

That the Go-Tokudaiji Minister had ropes stretched on his main hall so that kites would not perch there, and that Saigyō, seeing it, said 'What harm would a kite perching there do? This lord's heart is only that much', and after that did not visit: I had heard this, and

when once ropes had been strung on the ridge of Kosaka-dono, where the prince of Ayanokōji lives, that precedent came to mind; but when someone told me, 'Truly, crows were gathering and taking the frogs in the pond, and he saw it and was saddened', I thought, 'Then it is splendid'.
For the Go-Tokudaiji (Minister) too, what reason might there have been?

notes.text: In Buddhist terms the whole world is a 'temporary lodging', and a house even more so. Kenkō knows that, and he still cares about houses. The tension runs through the whole section.
{心|こころ}にくし again (see sections 4 and 150): admirable, and makes you curious about the owner. こそ … ゆれ: the realis form of ゆ ('looks').
{唐|から}: China, and in general the continent. Imported Chinese objects were the luxury goods of the time.
Fires were frequent in the capital, and wooden mansions burned down often. 'Smoke in a moment' is literal, and also a picture of impermanence.

Fujiwara no Sanesada (1139–1192), a high minister and a good poet. Saigyō (1118–1190), the wandering poet-monk, was one of the most loved poets of Japan. Saigyō had once been a warrior in the service of Sanesada's family, the Tokudaiji, which makes his snub sharper. The translation uses Sanesada's name instead of his title.
Usually identified as Prince Shōe, a son of Emperor Kameyama who had become a priest. Ayanokōji is a street in Kyoto, not a name; Kosaka-dono was his residence. He lived in Kenkō's own time.

notes.quote: この殿の御心さばかりにこそ
notes.text: 'This lord's mind is only that big.' Saigyō's verdict on a man who could not share his roof with a bird. こそ with the end left out (…あらめ).

notes.quote: さてはいみじくこそとおぼえしか
notes.text: The twist: the same ropes, but this time to protect frogs. So Kenkō is not sure any more about Sanesada, and the section ends with a fair question instead of a verdict. し, しか: the past auxiliary き, for things he experienced himself.
